detail.abstract: How much is a better rating worth in terms of price? The question matters for both hosts and platforms, but it is hard to answer using market data. This is because better listings collect better reviews and also charge more. This paper uses search logs from Jabama, an Iranian short-term rental platform, which record the listings each user saw, their order and price, alongside the one the user booked. The same listing appears in many sessions at different prices, so its persistent unrecorded quality can be held fixed, and its rating is read together with the number of reviews behind it. Without these controls, users look far less sensitive to price; with them, they are about five times as price sensitive. A 0.2-star rating gain raises a listing's booking probability by more than a 5 percent price cut does (20.0 against 14.3 percent). Ten extra reviews at the same average rating are worth about twice as much to a thinly reviewed listing as to a frequently shown one (25.0 against 11.9 percent), so the first reviews matter most. These comparisons let hosts and the platform weigh reputation against price. The price effect is causal under conditions that hold only approximately and is likely conservative; the reputation effects rest on stronger assumptions. All results describe how a booking is shared among the listings the platform displayed.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is taking over tasks that knowledge workers do. How many of the jobs they lose can manual work replace? A model of the U.S. labor market follows people who initially hold or seek knowledge jobs as the share of knowledge tasks that AI can perform rises from 5 to 35 percent over six years. Whether they have work depends far more on how much of the income from AI is spent than on whether they qualify for manual jobs. In the main experiment, capital owners spend half of any income they gain, interest rates do not fall, and adopting AI requires little investment. Spending and output fall, and jobs become harder to find in knowledge and manual work. Over twenty years, the rise in their manual employment makes up for 40 percent of the fall in their knowledge employment. A further 2.4 percentage points of them are without work, and the manual wage is 22 percent lower. If capital owners gradually spend all of a lasting income gain, the figure is 60 percent, and 1.3 points more are without work. Letting every knowledge worker qualify for manual jobs changes who holds those jobs and lowers the manual wage, but changes the share without work by at most 0.1 point. An interest rate that falls when the economy is weak only delays the shortfall in spending. Paying residents half of the rise in AI licence income does less for employment than the interest-rate response, but protects household consumption better.

detail.abstract: When firms acquire technology businesses, they acquire intellectual property alongside established inventor collaborations. We examine whether historically active inventor-name pairs within Chinese acquisition targets are more likely to appear together on patents filed after completion. The analysis covers 27,591 preacquisition pairs from 545 acquisitions drawn from 725 candidate transactions. Within three years after completion, 3,920 pairs (14.21%) appear together on filings under the targets' original legal names or documented aliases. In acquisition fixed-effects regressions controlling for pre-deal breadth across International Patent Classification subclasses (IPC4), a one-unit increase in ln(1 + pre-acquisition joint applications) is associated with a 12.22-percentage-point increase in observed recurrence (standard error 0.0176). With a control for collaboration recency, the corresponding estimate is 9.79 percentage points (standard error 0.0161). Historical joint-patenting intensity thus predicts which inventor-name pairs continue to appear together on target-associated patent filings after acquisition.

detail.abstract: Standard auction theory assumes that inviting an additional bidder to participate in an auction does not interfere with existing bidders' ability to submit bids. However, this assumption may fail in digital ad auctions that implement header bidding where all advertising partners are solicited simultaneously, since each additional bid request consumes browser-side processing and network time and can cause bids to arrive too late to compete. We study whether a publisher can improve display advertising revenue by reducing the size of the solicited partner set due to this "latency externality." We report the results of a large-scale field experiment conducted in collaboration with a major digital publisher over 20 days and 4 websites. During the experimental period, 17.8 million user browsing sessions were randomly assigned to either the status quo or control condition, where the publisher's full set of 13 demand partners were invited to bid for available ad auctions, or to a treatment condition where the 5 partners with the weakest pre-experiment performance were dropped from the solicited set. Analysis of detailed auction-level data reveals that the treatment increased the average percentage of solicited partners returning "valid bids" (i.e., that met the bid floor and arrived on-time) from 24.6% to 34.7% and lowered the percentage of auctions with no valid bids from 34.9% to 30.9%. The average valid bid amount also increased from $0.935 to $1.075 per thousand impressions, with the effect driven primarily by the removal of lower-quality partners who tended to submit lower bids. Among the retained partners, the treatment also resulted in a smaller and marginally significant increase in average valid bid amounts, consistent with higher bids having slower average response times and therefore benefiting the most from latency relief. On the publisher side, the treatment increased average revenue per thousand sessions (RPS) by 1.4% and average revenue per thousand pageviews (RPM) by 1.3%. This effect was mainly driven by a 1.0% increase in average filled impressions per session, while the average price paid per impression and user engagement remained unchanged. By quantifying the tradeoff between partner removal and latency relief, our findings suggest that the selection of partners to solicit is a key design choice in online ad auctions and that less can be more when it comes to the size of the solicited demand partner set.

detail.abstract: The expansion of distributed Internet of Things (IoT) networks has increased the number of connected devices, communication paths, and points at which malicious activity can enter a system. Conventional perimeterbased security and isolated intrusion detection systems are increasingly difficult to apply where devices differ in computing capacity, ownership, location, and communication behaviour. This article critically examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain can be combined to strengthen threat detection and security management in distributed IoT environments. It synthesises research on machine learning, deep learning, federated learning, intrusion detection, blockchain-based access control, trust management, and secure device onboarding. The review identifies complementary roles: AI can analyse traffic and device behaviour to detect suspicious patterns, while permissioned blockchain can support tamper-evident event records, decentralised trust coordination, access-policy enforcement, and accountable sharing of threat intelligence. The article proposes a layered framework that places lightweight detection near devices, collaborative model training at edge or gateway nodes, and blockchain-based governance across participating domains. The analysis also identifies trade-offs involving latency, energy use, privacy, model poisoning, consensus overhead, and benchmark-data quality. Because no original experiment or dataset was supplied, the results reported here are findings from the reviewed literature and a conceptual synthesis, not newly measured performance. The article concludes that AI-blockchain integration is promising when functions are carefully separated and matched to network-layer capabilities, but it requires reproducible real-world validation before deployment claims can be made.

detail.abstract: Maladaptive behaviour in schools and workplaces arises from the interaction of individual regulatory capacities, stress, social influences, and organisational conditions. This conceptual and integrative paper examines how cognitive self-regulation, emotional control, psychological stress, social context, leadership, and safety culture contribute to behavioural risk, and analyses how artificial intelligence, machine learning, and behavioural analytics might identify psychological risk indicators and potential safety-related outcomes. Applications considered include student behavioural assessment, school counselling, employee safety monitoring, occupational health, and AI-supported early intervention. The paper also considers technological risks arising from communication failures and cybersecurity weaknesses, and critically addresses data privacy, algorithmic bias, psychological profiling, explainability, informed consent, ethical monitoring, and the limits of behavioural prediction. Two tables and two figures summarise risk indicators, ethical safeguards, a person-in-context model, and an integrated predictive framework that links psychological assessment, behavioural intervention, organisational support, and AI decision support. No new empirical data are reported: established evidence is distinguished from proposed models, and the framework is offered as a hypothesis requiring validation. The paper concludes that prediction should support, and never replace, human assessment, counselling, and supportive leadership.

detail.abstract: This research note examines the empirical relationship between reported automated detection and reported automated decision-making across the first 38 monthly aggregate releases of the European Union Digital Services Act (DSA) Transparency Database (25 September 2023 to 31 October 2026; 43,463,346,962 published Statements of Reasons across 278 named platforms). Across the cumulative aggregate, 93.86% of statements report automated detection, whereas 54.50% report fully automated decision-making, 9.60% partially automated decision-making and 35.90% non-automated decision-making—a 39.35 percentage-point gap between automated intake flagging and full decision automation. In the joint 2x3 contingency table, 34.50% of automatically detected statements (14.07 billion records) are recorded as non-automated at the decision stage. Provider-level decomposition shows that unweighted EU totals are heavily shaped by extreme concentration: Google Shopping accounts for 76.95% of all published statements and 94.96% of all non-automated decision records. Across the remaining 277 platforms (10.02 billion statements), a 34.65 percentage-point gap persists between automated detection (85.14%) and fully automated decisions (50.49%), while partially automated decisions account for 41.66% and non-automated decisions for 7.85%. All results are descriptive accounting identities over provider-submitted administrative records; statutory 'automated means' does not establish artificial-intelligence use, review quality or DSA compliance.

detail.abstract:
The widespread adoption of lightweight operating systems has transformed modern cloud native computing. Alpine Linux has emerged as one of the most common container base images due to its small footprint, reduced dependency structure, and operational efficiency. While these design decisions provide significant benefits, they may also alter system dependencies in ways that influence security behavior. 

     This paper examines CVE-2026-123158 through a systems engineering lens. Rather than treating the issue solely as a software vulnerability, the study investigates how architectural decisions, dependency structures, implementation assumptions, and stakeholder perspectives interacted to produce a security-relevant outcome. A reproducible Alpine Linux 3.15 environment consisting of OpenSSH, musl libc, and a Flask web application was constructed to reconstruct the relevant authentication architecture. Additional experiments were performed against musl's implementation of crypt() to evaluate behavior near password-length boundaries discussed in public analyses of the vulnerability. 

     The findings suggest that the observed behavior is best understood as an emergent property of the overall system rather than the failure of an individual component. The study demonstrates how minimalistic architectural goals can alter authentication dependency structures and highlights the value of systems-engineering methods when evaluating security-critical infrastructures.

detail.abstract: Unsafe workplace behaviour and occupational ill health arise from interactions among individual cognition, psychological stress, motivation, leadership, organisational culture and technical conditions. This paper offers a conceptual synthesis of how artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning and behavioural modelling can identify human-factor risks, predict unsafe behaviour and support occupational health and safety decisions. Drawing on seven supplied sources and eight additional peer-reviewed works, it examines cognitive regulation and self-control, safety motivation, safety-specific leadership and safety climate, and links them to AI applications including wearable sensors, computer vision, anomaly detection, predictive risk scoring and decision-support systems. It then considers how network disruption, latency, packet loss, unreliable emergency alerts and cybersecurity threats can undermine digital safety systems. Applications in oil and gas, manufacturing, construction, healthcare and other high-risk settings are evaluated, together with privacy, surveillance, algorithmic bias, explainability, data reliability and human oversight. The paper proposes an integrated predictive framework and five testable propositions. Established evidence is distinguished from proposals, and no new empirical data are reported.

detail.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed during flood events to assess inundation, monitor infrastructure and support emergency response, but it is still unclear how far documented deployments go beyond producing imagery. Earlier reviews pooled field campaigns with simulations, benchmark datasets and concept papers, which makes it difficult to distinguish demonstrated field applications from experimental or conceptual capabilities. Following PRISMA 2020, we screened 1,815 unique Web of Science and Scopus records and, after full-text eligibility checks, included 182 studies in which a UAV was flown in connection with an identified flood event or flood-affected site; 133 of them document flights during or after a specific flood. Each study was coded by infrastructure system or emergency service, flood phase, sensing and analytics, evidence type and a five-level operational maturity scale running from field acquisition to measured outcomes. Post-flood work dominates (122 studies), and water and drainage assets (135) and transport (65) are the systems most often observed; electricity (6) and sanitation (2) are barely represented. UAV-mounted RGB cameras were the predominant sensing technology (164 studies), with structure-from-motion (SfM) photogrammetry the most commonly reported processing technique (99 studies), while UAV-mounted LiDAR, thermal infrared cameras and multispectral cameras were each reported in fewer than 10% of studies. Nearly three-quarters of the studies (72.5%) stop at field acquisition, and only 13 document timely delivery to responders or a specific decision taken with UAV outputs. None of the included studies reported an evaluation of the effects of UAV-informed decisions on response or recovery outcomes. Latency (4.9%), operation under degraded communications (1.1%), multi-sensor fusion (5.5%) and repeat monitoring (17.6%) are rarely reported. Only 13.2% studies were conducted in explicitly urban settings, also highlighting the limited direct evidence available for assessing UAV operational maturity in urban infrastructure systems. We argue that urban flood resilience now depends less on new sensors than on decision-validated, cross-system and longitudinal field programmes, and we set out a research agenda for building them into city emergency and recovery systems.

detail.abstract:
This working paper was prepared for the National Bank of Belgium’s biennial research conference on “Fiscal-monetary policy interactions in the 21st century”, held on 8–9 October 2026.

We develop a decomposition of debt-to-GDP dynamics that distinguishes inflation compensation, real interest rates, and compensation for bearing interest-rate and sovereign risk. Using security-level data from the Eurosystem’s Securities Holdings Statistics, we apply it to the five largest euro-area sovereign issuers. We find that low ex ante real interest rates relative to real GDP growth substantially reduced debt ratios, whereas short-term inflation surprises contributed only modestly. Compensation for interest-rate and sovereign risk was economically important and varied markedly across countries and over time. News about future inflation generated sizeable return surprises, driving a wedge between realised returns and the compensation for interest-rate risk priced ex ante. Finally, central-bank bond holdings transferred interest-rate and sovereign-risk exposure from private investors to the consolidated public sector. This transfer initially reduced consolidated debt ratios, but subsequently raised them as policy rates and bond yields increased.

detail.abstract:
This working paper was prepared for the National Bank of Belgium’s biennial research conference on “Fiscal-monetary policy interactions in the 21st century”, held on 8–9 October 2026.

The maturity of government debt affects inflation when bond-market arbitrage is limited. We develop a tractable model in which risk-averse arbitrageurs absorb duration risk, generating a term premium that rises with the supply of long-term debt. Lengthening maturity therefore raises the return on government debt relative to the policy rate. We show analytically that the resulting inflation dynamics depend on the monetary–fiscal regime. Under monetary dominance, inflation falls at every horizon despite monetary easing. Under fiscal dominance, inflation falls on impact but later turns positive, leaving the price level permanently higher. Lower bond prices require the initial deflation to maintain fiscal solvency, while higher borrowing costs eventually require inflation. In a calibrated New Keynesian model, a persistent lengthening of debt duration by one month raises the term premium by 17 basis points, lowers inflation by almost 0.2 percentage points, and contracts output under both regimes. Inflation takes around five years to turn positive under fiscal dominance.

detail.abstract: Pharmaceutical supply-chain disruptions impose severe clinical and operational burdens on United States healthcare systems, yet hospital pharmacies largely manage shortages reactively after shelves empty. This paper presents a two-layer predictive early-warning framework designed to manufacture actionable lead time before national supply disruptions reach the dispensing point. Layer 1 estimates product-level shortage probabilities across 4-, 8-, and 12-week horizons using publicly available federal regulatory, manufacturing, and pricing signals. Layer 2 integrates those probabilities with an individual organization's local utilization velocity, inventory days on hand, clinical criticality, and therapeutic substitution difficulty to generate a weekly, prioritized watch list. To establish operational feasibility and transparent evaluation benchmarks, this paper details the mathematical formulation, an open-source Python reference implementation, pipeline verification on a 12-product illustrative reference dataset, and target validation thresholds (4-to 8-week lead time and top-tier precision) governing institutional pilot deployment. Designed for hospital pharmacy departments, health systems, specialty pharmacies, and regional distributors, the methodology relies entirely on public data for market risk scoring, enabling scalable, zero-mandate adoption across the U.S. healthcare supply chain.

detail.abstract: In our game-theoretic framework, competing AI firms choose whether to rush model development or slow it to improve safety. The combination of the gains from leading and the costs of falling behind can generate a prisoner's dilemma in which both firms rush in equilibrium, although this is suboptimal. There can also be multiple Pareto-ranked equilibria in which both firms rush, or both firms slow down. By increasing misalignment risk, rushing can generate negative externalities which amplify the wedge between equilibrium and optimal outcomes. Fining misalignment can restore firms' incentives to slow down if moral hazard and limited liability constraints are not too tight. Monitoring by embedded observers can mitigate these constraints. An extension to competition between countries shows that international coordination can be facilitated or hindered by embedded external observers, depending on their impact on technology transfers.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author through Hikari Analytics.

detail.abstract: Range bars close when price has moved a set distance, not when a clock ticks. We study a percentage version on E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) futures: a bar seals when its high-to-low ratio reaches a fixed quantum, so a "50e" bar is always 0.25% of price tall. This keeps bars comparable while NQ rose six-fold, from about 4,900 to over 29,000. Using about one billion trade records from January 2017 to October 2026 (146,700 bars at 0.25% and 889,231 at 0.10%), we ask one question: can the colour of the next bar be called better than a coin? Across a ledger of 804 logged trials - Markov chains, hidden-state models, boosted trees, a convolutional network on chart images, over a hundred preregistered indicator rules, trend filters, topological features, intrabar timing and blind chart reading by a language model - the answer is no. Out-of-sample hit rates sit near 50%, inside null bands from shifted labels, random bars on the same days and within-day shuffled paths. Apparent edges of 54-58% were artefacts. The largest came from "phantom" bars: one trade that jumps several levels writes a chain of same-colour bars lasting under a second. They are 0.93% of bars and cannot be traded; removing them erased both earlier passes. Indicators predict their own next step well, but equally well on shuffled paths. What the bars do measure is pace: a time-to-seal model explains about 70% of the variance of the next bar's log duration. One recent-period lead is reported as unconfirmed.

detail.abstract: When an officer hears a safety recording play on the bridge, what can the officer infer about a passenger listening one deck below? This paper examines that question through three accident investigations involving the ferries Grace Sparkes and Sam McBride and the cruise ship Hamburg. A structured comparison distinguishes evidence that someone issued a message from evidence that a particular audience could hear it, understand it, or act on it. Post-incident testing on Grace Sparkes revealed a fault that a listener at the steering station could miss. On Sam McBride, crowd noise and faulty speakers compromised a departure warning whose practical relevance came later in the crossing. On Hamburg, the master ordered a passenger announcement but could not understand its German wording. Together, the cases show why a useful account of a broadcast must identify the listener, the location and the moment at which the information mattered. They also show where retrospective evidence ends and a listening test would have to begin.

detail.abstract: The expansion of generative artificial intelligence makes it necessary to distinguish computational consumption, adoption, and problematic dependence. This article proposes Tokenaholics as an exploratory concept without diagnostic equivalence and combines an interdisciplinary critical review with secondary analysis of public aggregates from 2025 and 2026. It examines Anthropic usage profiles by country and occupational group, Vercel daily token and spending shares, and GitHub indicators. K-means using five variables selects a two-group partition among 121 countries, with limited separation (silhouette of 0.308). The GitHub-Anthropic comparison matches eight of the ten countries in the GitHub table. Computer and mathematical occupations have published shares of 23.80% in chat and 28.17% in the API in May 2026; these measures retain each channel's denominator. Temporal evaluation of Ridge and three baselines does not support stable predictive superiority. Budget scenarios for 2027 combine token quantity and effective price under a constant mix. The findings describe geographic heterogeneity, differences between channels, and distinct distributions of tokens and expenditure. These results characterize the sociotechnical context without operationalizing or validating Tokenaholics, estimating the prevalence of dependence, or identifying causality. The contribution to computer science is to connect a bounded conceptual definition with reproducible analytical procedures and a future agenda for evaluating regulation, verification, and functional impairment.

affiliations: University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Perceived Social Norms and Information Disclosure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Social-information messages are widely used to influence norm perceptions and norm-relevant behavior, but their effects may depend on what they report and how they are disclosed. This paper develops a belief-based framework connecting personal values and perceived social norms through inference about a latent appropriateness standard. The framework shows how messages affect perceived social norms, with potential implications for subsequent behavior, through two mechanisms: First, personalvalue and perceived-norm statistics encode previous participants' private information differently because perceived-norm reports also incorporate an inference about others' assessments. Second, relative to private disclosure, public disclosure also affects recipients' beliefs about others' assessments, as they expect other group members to update using the same statistic. These mechanisms imply that, for equally sized changes on the same scale, perceived-norm statistics induce larger shifts in current perceived norms than personal-value statistics, and that public disclosure induces larger marginal responses than private disclosure. Thus, the effect of a norm-relevant message can depend not only on the value it reports, but also on how the reported statistic is constructed and who is known to observe it.

detail.abstract: Intraday research often scores a condition by how often price touches a target in its declared direction within a fixed time. Under a time cap, touch probabilities can rise with volatility even without directional predictability, so a one-sided score can mix direction with movement. This paper measures both directions on the same events for 504 pre-specified conditions, 42 continuation states at four horizons and three target levels, on 295 U.S.-listed stocks and ETFs from July 2017 to December 2024, with 161.8 million one-minute event-horizon observations. A first pass found 38 conditions whose declared-direction reach was a Benjamini-Hochberg discovery at q = 0.10 and at least 25% above a matched unconditional rate. All 38 also reach the opposite target more often than their references, and 26 clear the same bar there. Paired on the same events, their shared elevation is resolved. None meets a follow-on screen for declared-minus-opposite asymmetry: 15 are pointwise equivalent within an exploratory tolerance of 10% of the baseline rate, and 23 are inconclusive. Events that reach exactly one of the two targets carry most of the extra reach. An in-sample recalibration of the reference on trailing relative volatility roughly halves the shared elevation. Among events that reach a target, the declared one comes first 51% to 53% of the time for 9 of the 38, against 50% in the reference, pointwise. Among the other 466 conditions, 12 pass the screen, but no condition passes a minimum-effect test against the tolerance. One-sided target reach is therefore not sufficient evidence of directional advantage, though the results do not show that the conditions lack directional or economic value. A synthetic check shows that the two-sided classification cannot separate added volatility from volatility plus drift. The results are development-period evidence, not out-of-sample validation.

detail.abstract: In a preregistered laboratory experiment, pairs negotiate face to face or via video in an ultimatum bargaining game over scarce or ample resources, with only the proposer knowing the stake. We find an efficiency-equity trade-off. All remote pairs reach an agreement, compared with 92% of face-to-face pairs. When resources are scarce, however, face-to-face pairs converge on an equal split, whereas remote divisions are far more unequal. This gap does not stem from more misreporting or suspicion. To understand it, we analyze conversations classified by a large language model and facial expressions measured by automated emotion recognition. Exploratory evidence suggests that strategic, distrustful negotiations, equally common in both media, still converge face to face but often derail remotely, especially when proposers display little distress. Without physical presence, the equal split loses its role as a shared reference point, which organizations moving negotiations online may need to supply.

detail.abstract: This article establishes the Sociology of Belonging as a foundational explanatory framework for human society understood as an evolutionary development of prehuman sociality and a historically organized, pathdependent system of relationships among differentiated individuals. It connects the evolutionary and psychological constitution of persons with the reciprocal organization of conceptual systems and institutional arrangements. Four philosophical principles guide the framework: Being Is Belonging, Belonging Is Always Imperfect, Dual Temporality (synchrony and diachrony), and the interdependence of material, biological, and institutional-human strata. Human belonging is analyzed through love, social significance, and existential significance; social significance is differentiated into interconnected integrative, economic, and power subsystems. Imperfect belonging creates enduring possibilities of tension and conflict, while differentiated agency and institutional mechanisms may convert conflict into creativity, collective learning, and adaptation. Social change is neither teleological nor necessarily progressive; divergent historical trajectories help explain cultural diversity. The article compares the proposed framework with major sociological traditions in two complementary ways: their responses to twelve fundamental sociological problems and their coverage of twenty theoretical dimensions. The comparisons identify substantial intellectual continuities and clarify the proposed integrative contribution without claiming that breadth alone establishes empirical superiority. The conclusion sets out a research agenda for testing the framework’s mechanisms, conceptual distinctions, and comparative explanatory value.

detail.abstract: We develop the theory of the Hausman test in the two-way error component model of Amemiya (1971), in which individual and time effects coexist. Exploiting the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix on four orthogonal projectors, we derive the variance of the within-GLS contrast in closed form, give the rank condition that fixes its degrees of freedom, and show that the contrast is a matrix-weighted combination of a between-individual and a between-time contrast. This yields separate and joint tests and an exact ordering among them. We establish the asymptotic null distribution of the feasible statistic, its consistency, and its local power under alternative asymptotic regimes, show that the conventional one-way statistic is not pivotal when time effects are present, and propose heteroskedasticity-robust and partial versions.

detail.abstract: Global product organisations make a promise to customers that extends beyond feature delivery: products should work dependably across intended users, markets, platforms and operating conditions. Keeping that promise is difficult when discovery, design, engineering, verification, suppliers and operations are distributed across locations and organisational boundaries. This paper examines the mechanisms through which global product teams can translate quality expectations into coordinated engineering action. It proposes the Global Product Quality Promise and Accountability Framework (GPQPAF), a conceptual framework linking customer expectation, product quality attributes, cross-functional decision rights, interface assurance, release evidence and field learning. The analysis distinguishes quality ownership from quality assurance, shared participation from collective ambiguity, and standardisation from uniformity. It also examines regional variation, supplier dependence, quality trade-offs, product lifecycle evidence and the role of leadership incentives. Three tables provide an accountability model, a risk-to-evidence matrix and a performance measurement framework. An implementation pathway and propositions for future evaluation are presented. The paper is conceptual and does not claim empirical validation; it offers a structured approach for organisations seeking to make product quality a shared and measurable promise.

detail.abstract: Rising order volumes, shrinking delivery windows, and the widespread adoption of automation have made warehouse decision-making increasingly dynamic, stochastic, and highdimensional. Exact optimization and metaheuristics lose efficacy under these conditions, as they assume static environments and require computationally expensive resolving whenever conditions change. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a promising alternative: it learns a policy offline and executes decisions via a forward pass of a neural network, without requiring an explicit system model. This paper presents a systematic literature review of DRL applications in warehouse operations. Following PRISMA guidelines, we synthesized 186 studies published between 2017 and 2026. We classify this literature across four operational domains: path planning, scheduling and task dispatching, inventory management, and battery management, and by their underlying DRL algorithm. Our review yields four principal findings: (1) value-based methods of the Deep Q-Network (DQN) family are the most frequently used, while Proximal Policy Optimization is the most widely used policy-gradient algorithm; (2) reported performance gains over classical methods range from about 4% to more than 50%, but are not comparable across studies because no common benchmark exists; (3) problem representation affects performance more than algorithmic choice; and (4) the domain remains highly simulation-based, lacking physical validation and safety certification. We conclude by outlining research directions, including average-reward formulations, industrial-scale multi-agent pathfinding, hybrid learning-search methods, and policy interpretability.

detail.abstract: The paper addresses the gap between theoretical explanations of economic cyclicity and its practical measurement: existing schools, from the classical economists and Keynesianism to neoclassical economics and debt theory, describe crises post factum but provide no operational criterion for their early identification. An approach based on the theory of macroeconomic cash gaps (MCG) is proposed, which transfers the tools of corporate budgeting (the cash flow budget) to the national level. Cyclicity is defined operationally as a change in the regimes of the cash gap balance: excess liquidity (> 0), financial equilibrium (= 0), demand deficit (< 0). It is shown that the Kitchin, Juglar and Kondratieff cycles differ only in the object of investment but follow the same logic of gap reproduction. Refined formulas are presented for the cash gap (taking into account depreciation and profit reinvestment) and its credit coverage (net of interest expenses). Calculations based on Russian data for 2007-2025 show that the cash gap balance reached –14.6% and -20.8% of GDP in 2024-2025 (-44,492 billion rubles in 2025) - a deep coverage deficit that forms the material basis of stagflation. A quantitative crisis criterion is proposed - a persistently negative balance exceeding 5% of GDP - with a distinction between recession, crisis and depression. The stagflation mechanism is revealed as a regular phase of the cycle: growing interest expenses (cost-push inflation) combine with credit contraction (stagnation); in the Russian economy this mechanism is reinforced by the tariff channel of state monopolies. A structural shift in GDP distribution is empirically confirmed: the capital share increased from 25 to 32.6%, the labor share fell from 75 to 67.4%, and the share of banks within capital rose from 14 to 43%. The Rogoff threshold is reinterpreted: the crises of 2008, 2015, 2022 and 2024-2025 occurred at a debt level of 41.6-72.2% of GDP, i.e. below the "magic" 90%; therefore, the threshold is not a constant but the condition whereby interest expenses exceed new credit issuance (Int ≥ ΔC). A forecast to 2050 (VAR/ARIMA) shows that under debt financing the 90% threshold is reached in 2027 or 2031, with debt/GDP rising to 163–181% by 2050; under emission-based financing, debt/GDP declines to 10-20%. The MCG theory does not reject previous schools but integrates them, providing a measurable indicator and an anti-cyclical regulation mechanism alternative to debt financing.

detail.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) inflicts an estimated $3.6 trillion lifetime economic burden on the United States, yet survivors in crisis face a fragmented emergency entry system. detail.abstract: Traders often describe prior highs and lows as "magnets" that pull price toward them. This study tests that idea on 2,103,840 one-minute Bybit BTCUSDT perpetual candles from 2021 to 2024, first as a forecast of which level price reaches next, then as a source of tradable entries. Around a 15-minute decision point with one candidate level above and one below, the nearer level was reached first in 71.91% of 7,085 resolved events. A driftless first-passage model that knows only the two distances predicts 70.46%, leaving a residual of 1.45 percentage points (month-block 95% interval [0.32, 2.61]). An exact-distance mirror placebo on the same price paths left 2.16 points [0.07, 4.34], larger when the near level was a previous-day high or low (8.79 points on 512 events). The residual was unstable across years and absent in trending conditions, and in walk-forward tests a model with trend and level-structure features did not improve on distance alone (log-loss change -0.00028, interval [-0.0018, +0.0011]). No entry design converted the destination signal into money: mean gross returns ranged from -8.9 to +8.3 basis points per trade against about 13 basis points of round-trip cost, and simple non-magnet confirmation placebos matched the best entry in money terms. Independent reconstructions, a target-aware exit diagnostic and a multi-asset machine-learning extension (BTC, ETH, XRP) reached the same conclusion. Where price goes next is largely a matter of distance, and knowing it did not pay.

detail.abstract: After the financial crisis, the largest U.S. banks cut their small-business lending sharply and never restored it. We ask what that retreat meant for rural America. Data reported under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) cover only about a third of rural small-business lending, because most rural lenders are community banks too small to report. We therefore estimate the originations of every nonreporting commercial bank from its Call Report holdings of small loans, allocate them to counties by its deposits, and validate the method against small banks that did report before 2005. Community banks make two-thirds of rural small-business loans and four-fifths in completely rural counties. Banks with $50 to $250 billion in assets in 2007 cut their rural lending by 66 percent between 2005-07 and 2016-19, more than their metropolitan lending, but they held only 8 percent of the rural market. Rural lending fell 41 percent in real terms over the same years, close to the metropolitan decline of 43 percent, and community banks account for 24 of the 52 points of gross rural decline. Measured against the number of small businesses, rural lending lost ground to metropolitan lending before 2005, in the years of bank consolidation. Since then rural dollars per small business have held up, while rural counties have received relatively fewer of the smallest loans. CRA data alone tell a different and misleading story, and CRA's one rural-specific incentive, the designation of distressed and underserved nonmetropolitan tracts, does not raise small-business lending.

This study investigates shifts in Bitcoin's return dependence across defensive and growth equity styles around the launch of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) on January 11, 2024. Using 1,459 daily returns synchronized to the 16:00 Eastern Time New York Stock Exchange close from December 31, 2020 to October 23, 2026, we examine dynamic correlations and conditional regression slopes between Bitcoin and five liquid exchange-traded funds (USMV, XLU, SPY, QQQ, and GLD). Statistical inference is evaluated using moving-block and stationary bootstraps, Newey–West regressions, a post-halving decomposition, and six pre-launch placebo tests.

Our empirical findings show that Bitcoin's bivariate correlation and conditional sensitivity increased with broad-market equities (SPY) and high-beta growth equities (QQQ), but compressed toward zero with defensive equities (USMV, XLU) and alternative safe-haven gold (GLD). After controlling for broad-market movements, the independent shift in Bitcoin's sensitivity to QQQ is no longer statistically significant, indicating that QQQ's increased co-movement primarily reflects its high market beta (~1.35) during a broad equity rally rather than an isolated technology-specific integration. In contrast, zero-investment defensive-minus-growth equity return spreads exhibit persistent and statistically significant negative shifts across all model specifications, including specifications controlling for broad-market exposure. These results demonstrate that conditioning on equity style is essential for multi-asset portfolio diversification and risk management, capturing conditional regime associations amid cryptocurrency institutionalization rather than an isolated causal treatment effect.

detail.abstract: I study the 2023 U.S. Medicaid "unwinding", the largest involuntary insurance coverage loss in the program's history, in which roughly 25 million Americans were disenrolled as states resumed eligibility renewals suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic. Exploiting staggered renewal timing and cross-state variation in pre-policy adult Medicaid enrollment, I estimate differencein-differences effects on Medicaid coverage, labor markets, crime, and mortality. detail.abstract: In a multidivisional firm, units must frequently transfer resources to each other to address unforeseen contingencies. Yet, the organization typically lacks the information to enforce unscheduled resource transfers, and divisions lack the budgetary discretion to pay for them. We model interdivisional cooperation as a "favor-exchange" agreement in which a division's manager may transfer resources to another division in the hope of being a receiver in the future. We show that by reassigning managers to roles over time, the organization can facilitate internal favorexchange agreements. We derive conditions under which role rotation makes the promise of interdivisional favor exchanges more credible by increasing the managers' future rewards from cooperation (rotation across divisions) or the punishment they suffer after defection (rotation in and out of superior positions). We discuss empirical implications of the model, as well as applications to other kinds of organizations such as government agencies, buyer-supplier relationships, and strategic alliances.

detail.abstract: This article critically compares the Anthropology of Belonging with four distinct traditions in cultural and symbolic anthropology: Lévy-Bruhl’s collective representations and participation, Lévi-Strauss’s relational analysis of symbolic structures, Mead’s investigation of cultural formation and personality, and Evans-Pritchard’s contextual interpretation of belief and social order. The comparison recognizes their indispensable demonstration that human experience is mediated by inherited meanings while rejecting the inference that symbolic coherence entails empirical truth, equitable institutional participation, or beneficial belonging. The proposed framework distinguishes material, biological, and institutional-human strata; reciprocal but analytically distinguishable conceptual systems and institutional arrangements; three pathways of belonging—love, social significance, and existential significance—and integrative, economic, and power subsystems within social significance. It further connects imperfect belonging and dual temporality to dynamic synchrony, social homeostasis, and disruptive diachrony. Social change may originate in conceptual interpretations or institutional practices, propagate across multiple dimensions, and yield simultaneous gains and losses. Neither cultural complexity nor scientific advancement supplies a universal ranking of societies or a necessary historical trajectory. By differentiating meaning, causal adequacy, institutional enactment, and uneven lived consequences, the article consolidates the four comparisons into a historically contingent, multidimensional research program without attributing to these authors positions they did not hold.

detail.abstract: Theory-driven computational psychiatry seeks to explain clinically relevant behaviour through generative models of latent cognitive and neural processes. Its translational use is limited, however, when distinct mechanisms generate similar observations, when parameters cannot be recovered reliably, or when uncertainty about a fitted model changes the intervention that would be recommended. This paper develops a mathematical framework that connects these problems rather than treating them as separate stages of a modelling pipeline. First, we define observational distinguishability across a family of experimental conditions and relate local parameter identifiability to the kernel of the Fisher information matrix. We show that independent measurement modalities resolve local non-identifiability precisely when their information nullspaces have trivial intersection. Second, we distinguish observational equivalence from clinical decision equivalence: models can be difficult to distinguish statistically while nevertheless implying different optimal decisions, or can disagree mechanistically without changing the optimal decision. Third, we prove a stability bound for optimal interventions under Wasserstein perturbations of predictive distributions. Under uniform strong convexity of the decision objective and a Lipschitz condition on its action gradient, the distance between optimal interventions is bounded linearly by the Wasserstein distance between the corresponding predictive laws. Finally, we formulate a decision-focused sequential experimental design criterion and a distributionally robust intervention problem. The results provide a mathematical bridge from model degeneracy and parameter uncertainty to treatment-relevant uncertainty. The framework is theoretical: clinical effectiveness is not asserted, and empirical implementation requires clinically validated outcome measures, causal assumptions, and prospective evaluation.

detail.abstract: This article reassesses seven major contributions to the study of human sociality from the standpoint of the Anthropology of Belonging. Its argument is deliberately asymmetrical: biological evolution explains the emergence of capacities that make human social relationships possible, but the history of societies is not itself a biological evolutionary process and has no necessary tendency toward progress, greater complexity, or Western institutional convergence. Cultural evolution is retained only as the established name of a research tradition; the institutional phenomena discussed here are described as historical reproduction, adaptation, transformation, regression, and discontinuity. Two explanatory reductions are rejected. Biological reduction treats society as though it were another organism and overlooks conceptual systems, institutional arrangements, and the speed of their reorganization. Rationalist-developmental reduction identifies growing knowledge, technological sophistication, economic output, or institutional differentiation with better human belonging, neglecting attachment, recognition, existential significance, and the unequal distribution of participation. The proposed framework connects four ontological principles, three pathways of belonging, and three interacting institutional subsystems with a theory of dynamic synchrony, social homeostasis, and disruptive diachrony. Comparative discussions of China, Egypt, Persia/Iran, African and Arab societies, and the United States illustrate uneven and non-teleological institutional outcomes without treating internally diverse regions as homogeneous. The article reformulates the contributions and limits of Darwin, Boyd and Richerson, Henrich, Sterelny, Tomasello, Hrdy, and de Waal; revisits primary, traditional, and contemporary Western analytical configurations; and proposes empirical tests that distinguish technological or economic gains from improvements in belonging. Its distinctive contribution is an integrated account of why biological capacities and cultural inheritance coexist with radically divergent, unequal, sometimes regressive institutional histories.

detail.abstract: We study the political economy of stakeholder governance and corporate lobbying. Lobbying shifts policy toward outcomes that increase the firm's profitability, but it also provokes a backlash from advocacy groups, which push policy back toward the median citizen's preferred outcome. When lobbying is opaque, this backlash generates a ratchet effect: lobbying and backlash escalate, fueling political polarization and instability with little or no policy gain for the firm. To buy quiet, firms adopt stakeholder governance, delegating lobbying to a manager who places less weight on profits and more on citizens' welfare and therefore lobbies less. When the conflict between the firm and society is small, stakeholder governance leads to more socially responsible policies without sacrificing the firm's profits. Paradoxically, when the conflict is large, delegating to a more socially minded manager benefits the firm at society's expense, producing more extreme, socially harmful policies, even when the delegation creates no new agency problems. Our results suggest that stakeholder governance can have unintended political consequences and offer novel implications for corporate governance and lobbying regulation.

detail.abstract: The Hausman (1978) test is the standard device for choosing between fixed and random effects in panel data, yet most of its theory, software defaults, and applied practice rest on the one-way error component model. This article reviews the literature on Hausman-type specification tests and organizes what is known about their extension to the two-way model of Wallace and Hussain (1969) and Amemiya (1971), in which individual and time effects coexist. Using the spectral decomposition of the two-way covariance matrix as a unifying device, we review the classic one-way results, the PMG-MG test in dynamic heterogeneous panels, the non-equivalence result of Kang (1985), and recent regression-based and Hausman-Taylor approaches. We show that a systematic theory of the generalized statistic is still missing and set out a research agenda: its analytical structure, separate tests for individual and time effects, asymptotics under alternative regimes, robust and partial versions, and empirical assessment in African panels.

detail.abstract: Human communication is structurally prone to risk: between the sender's intention and the receiver's interpretation, there always emerges a gap in meaning, one that is filled through inference, prior assumptions, and unstable contextual frameworks. This article provides a 2025 assessment of uncertainty in communication, with particular emphasis on the Romanian political landscape. It brings together classical philosophical and linguistic perspectives with recent analyses of political, populist, and sovereigntist discourse. The study examines the cognitive and discursive mechanisms that generate uncertainty, the ways in which these mechanisms are instrumentalized by political and media actors, and the extent to which digital acceleration and geopolitical pressures are transforming public communication into a field of permanent tension. detail.abstract: This article compares the Anthropology of Belonging with Émile Durkheim’s analysis of solidarity and collective representations, Max Weber’s interpretive sociology of meaningful action and legitimate domination, and Anthony Giddens’s theory of structuration. Building on earlier comparisons developed within the Sociology of Belonging, it examines the anthropological problem of how historically diverse societies organize integration, reproduce institutions, and undergo transformation without following a necessary evolutionary sequence. The proposed framework distinguishes conceptual systems from institutional arrangements; three pathways of belonging—love, social significance, and existential significance; and economic, integrative, and power subsystems within social significance. Its ontological commitments include relational constitution, imperfect belonging, dual temporality, and differentiated material, biological, and institutional-human strata. The comparison finds substantive affinities with Durkheim’s emergent social order, Weber’s interpretive and historical analysis, and Giddens’s recursive account of agency and structure. The distinctive analytical proposal concerns the separation of institutional continuity from beneficial belonging and adaptability, and the explicit reconstruction of mechanisms through which conceptual or institutional changes produce multidimensional, contradictory, and potentially reversible outcomes. The article formulates a comparative research program rather than claiming that its integrative scope has already been empirically validated.

detail.abstract: Does dynamic calibration improve tail-risk forecasts, or mainly make them more conservative? This paper evaluates a dynamic joint calibration (DJC) rule for value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES) using US industry portfolios. In the evaluation specified before its results were computed, DJC outperforms daily batch calibration but does not significantly improve the uncalibrated equal-weight combination. Its advantage over an adapted online controller is sensitive to the inference specification. Exploratory analyses show that the gain over the uncalibrated forecast is concentrated in a few observations. A constant multiplier chosen with hindsight outperforms DJC in a historical yen sample. In simulations with correct base forecasts, DJC's one-sided updates lower violation rates below their nominal levels. On the US combination, sharing the VaR multiplier with ES also scores better than updating the two separately. These findings support evaluating calibration against uncalibrated forecasts and fixed or shared multipliers, while reporting predictive accuracy and conservatism separately.

detail.abstract:
This article compares the theories of Émile Durkheim and Talcott Parsons with the Sociology of Belonging to investigate the relationship between social integration, systemic reproduction, and institutional adaptability.

Durkheim explains social cohesion through solidarity, moral regulation, and collective representations. Parsons develops a theory of social systems emphasizing normative integration, functional differentiation, and institutional reproduction.

The Sociology of Belonging incorporates these contributions within an evolutionary and relational framework in which individuals are constituted through social relationships while remaining differentiated from the institutions that organize their lives.

The analysis focuses on imperfect belonging and dual temporality as theoretical principles connecting institutional stability with the permanent possibility of conflict, creativity, and transformation.

The article compares the three approaches across twelve fundamental sociological problems and twenty theoretical dimensions.

Its principal contribution is a conditional explanation of how social integration and institutional reproduction can facilitate or obstruct adaptability.

Institutional arrangements facilitate adaptation when they coordinate differentiated participation, protect criticism, permit experimentation, and enable the revision of established practices. Conversely, institutionalized conformity and concentrated gatekeeping may suppress feedback, delay institutional learning, and increase the costs of responding to changing circumstances.

The article argues that institutional stability and adaptability are neither inherently contradictory nor automatically complementary. Their relationship depends on identifiable mechanisms governing individual differentiation, authority, participation, and institutional revision.

The proposed framework generates comparative hypotheses concerning institutional openness, collective learning, and the capacity of societies to respond to endogenous and exogenous disturbances.

detail.abstract:
In clinical oncology pathology, diagnostic error penalties are profoundly asymmetric. While a false-positive classification subjects a patient to anxiety and secondary biopsy, a false-negative classification is potentially fatal, delaying critical oncological intervention and accelerating metastatic disease progression. Despite this extreme clinical asymmetry, contemporary deep learning diagnostic systems are predominantly evaluated using symmetric performance metrics and deployed with default decision thresholds (tau = 0.50). In addition, modern deep neural networks frequently produce overconfident, uncalibrated probability estimates that misrepresent true posterior malignancy likelihoods.
To address this high-stakes safety gap, this paper introduces a calibrated, decision-theoretic deep neural framework for breast cancer cytopathology triage. Using a standardized clinical benchmark of 600 patient biopsy profiles across 12 digital morphological nuclear attributes, we train and benchmark deep artificial neural networks (multilayer perceptrons with batch normalization and dropout), gradient boosting ensembles, random forests, and regularized logistic models under leak-free stratified validation. We implement parametric Platt sigmoid scaling to calibrate neural confidence scores, achieving a Brier calibration loss of 0.0209 and an Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (PR-AUC) of 0.9981. We then formalize a clinical cost-sensitive expected loss objective function parameterized by a 50:1 clinical loss ratio (C_FN = $25,000 vs. C_FP = $500). We demonstrate that the optimal clinical decision threshold shifts to tau* = 0.34, achieving 100.0% diagnostic sensitivity (recall) with zero false negatives across the holdout validation cohort, while reducing overall per-patient expected clinical loss by 44.9% ($245.83 vs. $445.83) compared to default thresholding. Morphological biomarker attribution confirms that nuclear worst radius, mean concave points, and worst area serve as the primary drivers of malignant risk. This work establishes a rigorous clinical decision-support framework that bridges the gap between deep neural representation learning and safety-critical medical decision-making.

detail.abstract: This article examines five major contributions to the anthropology of exchange and institutional organization—Bronisław Malinowski’s ethnography of reciprocity and obligation, Marcel Mauss’s theory of the gift, Karl Polanyi’s comparative institutional analysis of economies, Marshall Sahlins’s account of culturally constituted economic relations, and Jack Goody’s studies of production, kinship, literacy, and historical comparison—from the standpoint of the Anthropology of Belonging. It argues that exchange is never adequately explained as the movement of goods alone: it is constituted through conceptual systems and institutional arrangements and may simultaneously involve attachment, recognition, existential meaning, material provisioning, and authority. The proposed framework distinguishes material, biological, and institutional-human strata; three pathways of belonging—love, social significance, and existential significance—and three analytical subsystems within social significance: integrative, economic, and power. These distinctions preserve the insight that economies are socially organized while rejecting the inference that reciprocity necessarily benefits participants, that institutional integration entails justice, or that increasing complexity implies progress. Dynamic synchrony, social homeostasis, and disruptive diachrony illuminate reproduction, rupture, and historically contingent recombination. Transformations may originate in either conceptual systems or institutional arrangements, and gains in one dimension may coincide with losses in another. The article develops convergences, differences, a comparative synthesis, and a research agenda for evaluating who participates in exchange, under which obligations, with what asymmetries of power, and with what multidimensional consequences. Its central conclusion is that no institutional form, including market society, possesses a predetermined historical destiny.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the continuing usefulness of Homo economicus for understanding consumer behaviour in contemporary digital marketplaces. It traces the development of the rational economic actor through Adam Smith's broader account of human motivation, Bentham's utilitarianism, John Stuart Mill's methodological abstraction, and the later contributions of Pareto and Robbins. It then considers why rational-choice models remain useful for analysing decisions under scarcity and changes in incentives, while also examining the limits of treating rationality as a complete description of human behaviour. detail.abstract: On November 12, 2026, Jensen Huang resigned as President and Chief Executive Officer of Nvidia after 33 years. Over the next three trading days the stock lost about 10 percent, roughly $424 billion of market value, although nothing about the company's products, customers, or order book had changed. detail.abstract: The circular economy has emerged as an important approach to improving environmental sustainability, resource efficiency, and business competitiveness within the restaurant and food service industry. In Colombia, increasing concerns regarding food waste, organic waste generation, packaging consumption, and inefficient resource utilization have created opportunities for integrating circular economy practices into gastronomic business operations. This article examines the application of circular economy principles in Colombia's restaurant and food service industry, focusing on waste reduction, sustainable resource management, operational efficiency, and business performance. Drawing on an integrative review of scholarly literature, institutional reports, and relevant environmental policies, the study investigates how restaurants, catering enterprises, and food service businesses can adopt sustainable procurement, food surplus redistribution, recycling, composting, inventory optimization, and resource recovery strategies. Particular attention is given to the economic and environmental implications of circular business models, especially among small and medium-sized enterprises. The analysis also identifies structural challenges, including inadequate waste-management infrastructure, limited financial resources, insufficient environmental awareness, and weak monitoring systems. Furthermore, emerging opportunities associated with digital waste tracking, sustainable packaging, food donation networks, and organic waste valorisation are examined. The article argues that circular economy practices can improve business sustainability by reducing operational costs, strengthening resource productivity, and improving environmental performance. Effective implementation requires coordinated institutional support, entrepreneurial training, appropriate infrastructure, and measurable sustainability strategies across Colombia's restaurant and food service industry.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's chronic insecurity creates conditions of interpretive uncertainty in which visible social identities may acquire security significance beyond their evidentiary value. This study examines how visible religious identity can become associated with perceived security risk through processes of identity misrecognition, risk salience and securitisation. Hijab controversies are used as an empirical-discursive site for tracing this process, rather than treated as the substantive object of the study. Adopting a qualitative, interpretive documentary design, the study analyses scholarly, legal, governmental and reputable media sources across documentary trajectories in Lagos, Osun, Kwara and Oyo between 2013 and 2024. The analysis develops a process-oriented heuristic: Symbolic Visibility → Social Interpretation → Misrecognition → Risk Salience → Perceived Risk → Securitising Practice to explain how an observable identity may acquire security relevance without corresponding evidence of threat. The study finds that security meaning is not inherent in religious visibility but mediated by contextual interpretation and institutional practice. It argues that when identity becomes a proxy for threat, misrecognition can function as a security-governance failure, generating false positives, misallocated attention, weakened information flows and diminished institutional legitimacy. The study further develops ambient securitisation as a modest analytical heuristic for understanding how security meaning may accumulate through repeated associations, contextual narratives and institutional responses without necessarily constituting formal securitisation. It concludes that effective security governance requires not reduced vigilance but more discriminating vigilance: threat assessment grounded in behaviour, intent, capability, networks and corroborated intelligence rather than visible identity alone.

This working paper examines the joints between the IMO Code for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MSC.595(111), adopted 21 May 2026, non-mandatory) and the mandatory legacy framework it does not displace: COLREG, SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, the ISM and ISPS Codes, and national law. detail.abstract:
While intrahousehold labor reallocation can mitigate illness-induced labor supply losses, its effectiveness depends on labor complementarities within the household and seasonal variations in labor demand. Using four years of weekly panel data from rural Zambia, this paper examines intrahousehold labor responses to adult illness by gender, season, and activity. The results reveal period-specific patterns of labor reallocation between spouses during the main agricultural season, potentially reflecting differences in the nature of farm activities across different stages of the production cycle. In particular, wives reduce their farm labor hours in response to
husbands’ illness-induced work absences in December and January, suggesting complementarities in spousal labor during planting and fertilizer application. Overall, intrahousehold labor substitution is insufficient to fully offset illness-induced labor shortages. We also document reductions in boys’ and girls’ schooling time after illness-induced work absences by their fathers and mothers, respectively, during the rainy season, highlighting the negative spillovers of parental illness on children’s education.

detail.abstract: Clinical trial capital is released on the calendar and judged at the end. We ask when a failing program could have been stopped, what was knowable at that moment, and how much was still unspent. We define a unit, the unspent fraction at trigger, and apply it to one public dataset and three late-stage programs in wet age-related macular degeneration that failed. In each program a routine gate was reached with a usable read on the table, and capital moved without it, because no one had built a read in advance and no contract gave anyone the right to act on one. Across six retina programs, a phase 2 vision gain over control averaged 3.2 letters and fell to minus 0.7 in phase 3, mostly because the control arm rose. Three study budgets show that a fluid-based read costs about one percent of the phase 3 program it would protect, so the barrier is the false stop, not the price. We argue that the stop has to be built before phase 1, in a phase 0: a small biology-first study that establishes what will be measured and what result ends the program. We set out which forms of phase 0 need a regulatory filing and which do not, and propose a standard term sheet, the Clean Sheet, that ties each tranche of capital to a pre-specified read. Phase 0 does not stop a trial. It is what makes stopping possible.

detail.abstract:
Corporate bond markets have grown steadily, and this growth is often interpreted as firms shifting from bank to market finance. In the aggregate the shift looks smooth, but for individual firms it is not. Using national accounts for 36 countries and firm-level data for more than 50, we show that part of the growth is credit deepening. Where the financing mix does change, it changes within large firms, and in jumps: a firm's bond share rises when it issues, and new bank loans erode it unless the firm issues again. detail.abstract: Forest regulation is imposed on forest owners, but the innovation it may induce takes place in the mills that buy their timber. We study this vertical separation in a model with regulated timber supply, imports, and mills that choose timber-saving technology subject to knowledge spillovers. Regulation induces innovation if and only if mills' timber demand is price-inelastic, so the response is weakest where output reacts strongly to costs. Mills lose unless spillovers are implausibly strong, whereas forest owners gain when the price response exceeds their rent share, a condition that imports make harder to meet. Endogenous technology dampens the price response and reduces leakage. With knowledge as a stock, a set-aside always lowers the present value of mills' profits, while a rule that raises the growing stock increases it if the stock's marginal growth rate exceeds a threshold above the interest rate. Estimates for Sweden imply induced innovation in both pulp and sawmilling, but a much weaker response in sawmilling.

detail.abstract:
Generation Z (Gen Z) is a socially conscious and digitally savvy consumer segment that is becoming more and more focused on the brand's commitment to social justice, mental health support, and sustainability. However, despite increased corporate interest in socially responsible practices, little research exists explaining how the three of these dimensions affect Gen Z's understanding of brand authenticity and trust in a unified way. This study addresses this gap by discussing about the responsible brand actions and how responsible actions affect the authenticity and authenticity leads to the prediction of trust among Gen Z consumers in Bengaluru.

A quantitative and cross-sectional research design was adopted, a structured questionnaire was used with the sample size of 300 Gen Z respondents being between the ages of 18-28 years. Multi-item Likert scales were created and used to measure Social Justice Engagement, Mental Health Support, Sustainability Practices, Perceived Brand Authenticity and Brand Trust. Data was analysed by the structural equation modelling (SmartPLS 4) on reliability, validity, direct effects, and mediation relationships.

Findings indicate that all three dimensions of brand responsibility have a significant, positive effect on perceived brand authenticity with sustainability practices being the most effective. Perceived brand authenticity became a very powerful predictor of brand trust. Mediation analysis confirmed some partial mediating effect of authenticity between the dimensions of responsibility and trust, pointing to the suggestion that the reason why Gen Z trusts brands is not only because of the responsible action, but because of the authenticity of the action and its communication.

The findings underscore the importance of authenticity as a key mechanism by which brands are connected to trust formation among Gen Z. Brands seeking to build strong and valuable relationships with young consumers must show consistent, transparent and long-term commitments to social and environmental issues. The research provides some practical information to marketers who are trying to create meaningful, honest branding strategies which will fit in with Gen Z's ethical expectations.

detail.abstract:
This Article argues that current student speech doctrine — which is composed of the content-agnostic “substantial disruption” test of Tinker v. Des Moines Independent School District and a small handful of exceptions — fails to adequately capture both the theoretical foundations underlying the doctrine and many of the fundamental intuitions regarding student speech shared by courts and school administrators. At the heart of the doctrine’s shortcomings is the presumption that all student speech, outside of a few limited exceptions, is equally valuable and entitled to the same degree of constitutional protection. But if, as the Court has repeatedly stated, the primary theoretical justification for protecting student speech is the promotion of democratic education — preparing students for active participation in open democratic discourse — this justification broadly revolves around speech on matters of public concern, like the black armbands protesting the Vietnam War in Tinker itself. In other student speech contexts, however — like those involving speech regarding purely private matters, personal insults, or nonsense — this justification is considerably weaker or nonexistent.

School speech doctrine should therefore explicitly recognize that not all student speech is entitled to the same degree of protection. Rather, courts should extend distinct degrees of protection to three different categories of student speech: (1) student speech on matters of public concern, to which a stringent version of Tinker should apply; (2) student speech that is not on matters of public concern, to which a more deferential but still meaningfully protective version of Tinker should apply; and (3) discrete and delineated categories of “low-value” student speech, to which a highly deferential standard of review should apply. Such an approach would not only lead to more intuitively sensible results, but it would also more accurately capture the complex interactions at the heart of school speech doctrine between students’ speech rights, schools’ mission to provide democratic education while instructing students as to appropriate social norms, and the practical realities of running an educational institution efficiently and effectively.

Purpose:
Consumer behaviour of Millennials and Generation Z has been coined as “doom spending.” The uncertainty driven by anxiety on internal and external levels has given a behavioural nudge towards consumerism. Consequently, the researchers investigate the transformation in this spending behaviour. The objective of the article is to explore the drivers of doom spending and examine its psychological and behavioural aspects among Indian consumers.

Design:
Survey data was collected from 200 respondents in the age range of 20 to 50. Data was collected on three dimensions of spending by consumer- mental, emotional, and social. Additionally, in-depth understanding of these dimensions was received by collecting qualitative data. The data analysis included carrying out Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for arriving at the optimum variables within each dimension. Furthermore, content analysis was performed on the qualitative data set.

Findings:
The key results of the study reflect the consumption behaviour of both the generations inclining towards luxury spending predominantly influenced by peers. Moreover, it was also found that the external environment in the form of social and digital media enhances the internal parameters of sensitivity, stress, and impulsion towards consumerism. The key insights are explained by Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) model. The qualitative finding reveals ‘fear of future’ and ‘consumption as catharsis’ as major arguments for spending behaviour.

Originality:
This unique research demonstrates behavioural contradictions in fulfilment of SDG 12 of ‘responsible consumption’. The implications are relevant for policymakers to nudge the production towards sustainable spending of Millennials and Generation Z.
